prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, bringing the measurement of time and frequency to the 10^-18 level.

statement.case_for: I now prefer B037 and withdraw my round-1 B042 position. The deciding facts are two. First, my round-1 premise that Ye shared the 2005 prize was wrong: Hall and Hansch were the laureates, as Lindroth said, so Ye's recognition is not a repeat-recognition issue. Second, the credit for B037 is the best-resolved on the shortlist: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift of the clock transition while many atoms are interrogated at once, and Ye's group took the strontium lattice clock into the 10^-18 regime and used it for many-body and redshift measurements. Independent laboratories have reproduced and exceeded the accuracy, and the physics is controlled and well understood, with applications in centimetre-scale gravitational redshift tests, bounds on varying constants and dark-matter searches. As an instrument builder I judge this on whether the measurement capability is real, reproduced and enabling, and it is. I accept that my earlier preference for new classes of matter over improved accuracy was a taste, not a Statutes criterion; magic-wavelength trapping of ensembles is a distinct invention that neither the 2005 comb prize nor the 2012 ion-control prize contains.
statement.case_against: The AMO and precision-measurement field has been recognised often (2005, 2012, 2018, 2022, 2023, 2025), so a further clock prize can be read as incremental. The redefinition of the second has not been adopted, so the headline application is still prospective. Two names leave out NIST, PTB, SYRTE and other lattice-clock groups and the ion-clock community, and the question of whether Ye is credited for the lattice clock itself or for clock-comb integration and the accuracy frontier remains, so the citation must be narrow. B042 remains the more conceptually novel science, but its credit set is structurally incomplete with Zhang deceased, and I no longer think I can defend it as a clean allocation.

responses.point: Correction of the 2005 premise and the claim that the lattice clock is a conceptual step
responses.response: You were right and I withdraw the premise in my round-1 statement and my ranking of B037 sixth that partly rested on it. Ye was not a 2005 laureate, so there is no repeat-recognition issue. I also take your point that magic-wavelength trapping is a conceptual step in the control of internal and motional states and not just better metrology, and that the many-body effects in lattice clocks give a window on quantum many-body physics. That answers the chair question about a new principle for the Statutes criterion better than my instrument-builder prior did. I do not share your view that the field is overdue; I only say the adjacent prizes are not a bar.

responses.point: Ye's recognition as a perception issue, and the Higgs credit problem
responses.response: I agree that Ye's earlier association with the comb circle is a perception issue and not a bar, and I now agree that the citation must say what is honoured, namely the lattice scheme and its realisation at 10^-18, with ion clocks, NIST, PTB and SYRTE acknowledged in the text. On B006 you conceded that founders and project leaders are not the people who made the observation. I share that and, as someone from detector collaborations, I would not defend Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee as discoverers. I also recuse myself in spirit from advocating B006 given my background, and I keep it only as an alternative.

Your argument that the HgTe experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, so crediting Molenkamp while omitting those names is an asymmetry the committee must state openly, is what moved me. Zhang's death means it cannot be repaired later. I still agree with you that Z2 insulators are distinct from the 2016 topological-phase prize and that the quantisation of the helical edge is less clean than in the quantum Hall effect, so I treat the 2016 overlap as secondary and the credit asymmetry as decisive for my change. I would not oppose a B042 citation worded as you propose if the committee prefers it.

responses.point: Redefinition of the second and the narrow citation
responses.response: I accept your answer that the prize recognises demonstrated accuracy and independent reproduction in several laboratories, not the outcome of a metrological decision, so the pending redefinition is confirmation of maturity and not a reason to wait. I agree with your wording around the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime. Your own point about the share of the record between Ye's group and RIKEN, PTB, SYRTE and others is why I do not add a third name; the Statutes limit makes any additions arbitrary.

I still do not see a route to B005 given Tu's omission and the contested two-dimensional exponents, and your own acknowledgement that Tu is a real defect. On the clock, your question about a new principle is fair; my answer is that the new element is the magic-wavelength condition applied to a confined ensemble, which is a distinct idea and not only improved accuracy.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts Ye's credit as the lattice-clock accuracy frontier and many-body physics, with other groups acknowledged only in the text.
Whether the fifth-or-sixth AMO and precision-measurement recognition in two decades weighs against B037 for the rest of the committee.
Whether B042 could be made defensible with a citation that openly leaves out the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D work, which would reopen my choice.
Whether an expert view could identify decisive individuals for B006.
statement.conflict_note: I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. My CERN doctoral work and detector collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO+) give an affinity with experimental projects such as ATLAS and CMS (B006), which is now only an alternative, and I would defer to the committee on recusal for it. I withdraw the incorrect statement in my round-1 text that Ye shared the 2005 prize.
